This study focuses on the internal null controllability of a partial differential equation modeling population growth and dispersion. Unlike previous work, we examine a model with a birth rate that is dependent on the population size, rather than a logistic model. A key aspect of this research involves deriving an appropriate Carleman estimate for a related adjoint equation, which arises from a transformation of the original control system. This estimate serves as a crucial tool in proving the internal null controllability of the population dynamics. Specifically, we demonstrate that there exists a moment function associated with the population P, such that its time derivative is bounded by a constant times the magnitude of the control, and this constant can be arbitrarily small as the population size approaches zero. Consequently, we can show that, given any small positive number, there is a control that drives the population to zero in a finite time, with the magnitude of the population at any given time being less than the specified small positive number. This result holds for a population that occupies a finite area within a larger domain, and it remains valid as the population size approaches zero. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the birth rate and the controllability of the population dynamics. In particular, if the birth rate is greater than one, we can show that the population becomes uncontrollable, whereas if the birth rate is less than one, we can find a control that drives the population to zero in a finite time. Finally, we provide an example of a birth rate function that is not globally bounded but is nonetheless associated with an internally controllable population dynamics. In addition, we examine the controllability of the population dynamics when the birth rate is dependent on the population size and occurs within a randomly fluctuating environment. In this case, we show that the population becomes uncontrollable if the birth rate is greater than one, whereas if the birth rate is less than one, we can find a control that drives the population to zero in a finite time. A mathematical model simulating species migration and competition is adjusted to include a random disturbance, representing unpredictable environmental changes. The model, inspired by the elector model, accounts for a tradeoff between species' ability to colonize new areas and their effectiveness in competing with others for resources. Analyzing this model, researchers found that a community can either consist of a single dominant species or multiple species coexisting in different ranges, depending on the level of disturbance and spatial extent. They also identified three possible scenarios: a single species dominates everywhere, species coexist in a narrow range where competition and colonization balance each other, or a single species dominates a large area with smaller populations existing in a thin border. Additionally, we examine the transcendence properties of a particular transcendental number associated with an algebraic extension, showing that its degree is equivalent to the degree of the underlying algebraic extension. To break the 95\% CDM limit, effective operators that mediate dark matter interactions must be extremely rare.  We re-evaluate the significance of $e^+e^-\to \gamma \, \text{NP}$ production at Belle II's intermediate energy, considering both elastic and inelastic interactions.  For inelastic interactions, a new process, $\gamma \, \text{NP} \to \gamma \, \text{NP} \, \text{visible}$, becomes relevant.  We find that inelastic operators are generally more challenging to detect than inelastic ones.  However, for a specific case, with an invisible operator, we find a new signal, dark matter pairs produced through initial-state radiation in $e^+e^- \to \text{NP} \, \text{NP}$, which can be distinguished from dark mesons and might be detectable at Belle II for certain operator structures.  For a single-particle production process, $e^+e^- \to \gamma \, \text{NP}$, we find that even with 8$ \, \text{ab}^{-1}$ of luminosity, the significance for inelastic operators remains below 1, indicating that inelastic operators may evade detection at Belle II.  On the other hand, for pair production processes, with 8$ \, \text{ab}^{-1}$ of luminosity, the Belle II limit on inelastic operators will be stronger than the LHC limit for masses up to 25 GeV.  For dislocated operators, we find that Belle II will be less effective than LHC experiments, except for a specific case with a forward detector with a longer acceptance, where the Belle II limit on inelastic operators will be stronger than the LHC limit for masses up to 35 GeV.  We also find that the forward detector at Belle II is more effective at setting limits on inelastic operators when using a tagging method with $e^+e^- \to \text{NP} \, \text{NP}$, where the Belle II limit on inelastic operators will be stronger than the LHC limit for masses up to 50 GeV.  Finally, we propose a set of effective operators that could be relevant for dark matter and are difficult to distinguish from the standard model, even with a precise measurement at Belle II, such as the operator $|e \bar{\nu} \, \text{NP}|^2

A key feature of neural development is the interplay between cell division and migration, and a prominent example is interkinetic nuclear migration, where cell nuclei move between the inner and outer edges of the neuroepithelial tissue as they undergo mitosis and differentiate into specific neuron types. While this process is crucial for proper neural development, its underlying mechanisms and how it influences pattern formation and cell type distribution are not yet fully understood. In this study, we used high-resolution imaging to examine interkinetic nuclear migration in the developing zebrafish retina and found that rather than following a directional or oscillatory pattern, retinal cell nuclei migrate randomly, even when considering their location within the tissue or the orientation of the retinal surface. We also found that this diffusive migration is independent of the time it takes for cells to differentiate into specific neuron types, and that the distribution of cell types is determined by the time cells are present at their respective retinal locations rather than their origin within the tissue. We developed a mathematical model that simulates this random migration and accurately replicates the observed patterns of cell type distribution in the retina. This model highlights the significance of random migration in producing the complex patterns of cell type distribution in the retina, and suggests that it can be applied to other developing tissues that exhibit similar patterns of cell type distribution. A new code framework called ECF has been proposed to improve source separation problems in various image and video applications. This code structure provides a clear and organized framework for developing and comparing different decoding methods, as well as a straightforward way to evaluate and format decoding codes, which was particularly beneficial during the development of the MAIA compressor for video recovery. MAIA achieves state-of-the-art compression efficiency while maintaining high image quality, outperforming existing compressors in the PSNR metric while matching the compression ratio of the BTF dataset and surpassing the MCL-JC dataset. Furthermore, MAIA exhibits superior performance in demosaicing color images captured with CMOS sensors, recovering near-lossless images from 4 times the captured data, as demonstrated through subjective and objective evaluations using various sensors and images. The ECF framework and MAIA compressor source codes are available online for public use.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases can be significantly influenced by a small number of highly infectious individuals who have close contact with many others. These super-spreader events are often seen in the early stages of an epidemic, where a single person with a highly contagious form of the virus can transmit it to many others at a gathering or in a specific setting. Historically, we can point to examples such as the 1918 Spanish flu, where soldiers in close quarters were particularly affected by the epidemic. In mathematical modeling, researchers have used a simple compartment model to simulate the spread of the disease, but these models do not effectively capture the rapid transmission seen in super-spreader events. In contrast, a model that accounts for the re-infection of recovered individuals can better explain these events. In this study, we apply a compartment model to a hypothetical epidemic in a small population and find that it can result in a rapid increase in transmission rates in the early stages of the epidemic. We also find that a high transmission rate in the early stages of the epidemic can lead to a second peak in the number of infected individuals even after a vaccine becomes widely available. In a larger population, the transmission rate may decrease more rapidly as it is less likely for a single event to result in a large number of new infections. In this case, we see that a high transmission rate in the early stages of the epidemic may not necessarily lead to a second peak in the number of infected individuals even after a vaccine becomes widely available. In both scenarios, we find that a high transmission rate in the early stages of the epidemic can lead to a higher number of infected individuals if a vaccine is not available. In a larger population, we also find that a high transmission rate in the early stages of the epidemic can result in a large number of new infections at a single event, potentially leading to a super-spreader event. In this scenario, we estimate that a transmission rate of 0.05 in a population of 100,000 can result in 50 new infections at a single event. In contrast, a lower transmission rate of 0.001 in the same population would only result in fewer than 10 new infections at a single event. Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with its continuous linear operators that form a set, O. We are interested in identifying subsets of O that repeat infinitely and contain every operator in O, while also satisfying certain properties of cyclicity. In particular, we can show that for the set of compact operators, there are no cyclic collections. Conversely, in the context of C[0,1] vector spaces, we can find collections of compact operators that are both locally cyclic and globally cyclic. Furthermore, we explore how these collections can be extended to higher intervals, revealing a pattern of cyclicity for operator collections within C^n[0,1]. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between these collections and the properties of their associated vector spaces. Along the way, we establish a key theorem that characterizes the cyclicity of operator collections in terms of their compact operators and the vector space's topological properties. This is particularly significant for demonstrating that the set of compact operators is always locally cyclic within metrizable vector spaces. Finally, we provide a more general definition of cyclicity that applies to operator collections on arbitrary vector spaces, revealing that compact operators form a locally cyclic set that contains no infinite cycles unless the vector space has a specific pathological property. This property, in turn, can be ensured under the additional assumption of infinite dimensionality. This research expands upon the foundation laid by its predecessor, the 1969 paper by the same authors titled "Locally cyclic collections of operators". This current paper also draws inspiration from the 1973 paper by the same authors titled "Locally cyclic collections of compact operators". This work further builds upon the 2013 paper by the same authors titled "Cyclic collections of compact operators on Banach spaces" by generalizing its results from Banach spaces to more comprehensive vector spaces. Precise knowledge of vector magnetic fields is crucial for understanding and predicting solar eruptions. Inference methods, such as the "optimally combined" approach, have significantly improved the accuracy of inferred measurements by utilizing multiple observational data sets. However, these methods may inadvertently perpetuate biases in measurements, which can be particularly problematic if based on flawed assumptions about instrumental responses. This study investigates bias in inferred measurements of the Helioseismic and Magnetic Observation (HMI) vector magnetic field component, Bc, using a forward modeling approach with the Solar Optical Observatory (SOLO). By analyzing multiple observational data sets, we identify and quantify sources of bias, specifically an instrumental response effect caused by the large field of view of the HMI telescope. This bias is quantified as 50.7 nT in magnitude. We further demonstrate that this study's approach can be applied to other inference methods and provide guidance on alleviating this bias in Bc measurements. By correcting this bias, we find a mean reduction of 10.6 nT in the standard deviation of local correlation tracking (LCT) Bc spectra in the quiet Sun. This study highlights the importance of considering instrumental effects in inference methods and provides a framework for identifying and mitigating bias in inferred measurements of the solar vector magnetic field. This approach is particularly relevant for improving the performance of machine learning inference methods. This study's findings also underscore the need for accurate calibration of observational data sets and the importance of accounting for instrumental responses in forward modeling of the solar vector magnetic field. A significant challenge in simulating strongly interacting electrons using approximate neural network methods arises from the Hubbard sign problem, which necessitates the efficient representation of fermionic operators as complex-valued tensors. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel framework based on a new type of neural network, where the output tensors have complex entries but no internal complex weight. This approach is particularly effective for approximating functions with multiple discontinuities, and we demonstrate its efficacy by applying it to the solution of a strongly interacting, one-dimensional Hubbard model. Compared to other methods, our approach yields a significant improvement in accuracy for a given computational cost. Furthermore, we show that our framework can be applied to various other problems, beyond the Hubbard model. This approach can be implemented using existing neural network libraries with a minimal modification, and we provide the details of this implementation. This approach offers a promising avenue for addressing the sign problem in various contexts. This work is an extension of the paper titled Mitigating the Hubbard Sign Issue with Complex-Valued Neural Networks presented at the 2022 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. Given a non-erasing free monoid morphism σ, we establish that the subshift defined by the iterates of σ has a complexity that grows at a rate of at least L*N (within a constant factor L) relative to the complexity of the original subshift. Additionally, when σ is associated with a finite automaton, we show that the complexity growth rate is exactly the rate of a regular series related to the automaton, and, under specific conditions on the alphabet and the automaton, we demonstrate that the entropy of the subshift is greater than the rate of a specific polynomial, with a comparison to the entropy of the original subshift. When σ is a basis change for the free group F_r by another basis F_s, we establish that the entropy of the associated subshift is equivalent to the entropy of the original subshift, with a coefficient related to the dimensions of the free groups F_r and F_s. Notably, when the basis change is defined by a simple swap of generators within the same free group F_r, we find that the entropy of the associated subshift is a fixed, finite multiple of the entropy of the original subshift, with a specific calculation for the case of the free group F_2. Furthermore, we show that the topological entropy of the subshift defined by the iterates of a non-erasing free monoid morphism σ is independent of the choice of generating set for the free monoid. Lastly, we provide examples of basis changes for the free group F_r that result in an entropy growth of N^(1-r) or N^(r-1) within a constant factor, as well as an example of a basis change for F_2 with an entropy growth of N^(1-1) within a constant factor.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting to new situations without additional guidance, humans excel at cross-task generalization. To achieve similar performance in artificial systems, researchers have explored methods to conduct cross-task training with the assistance of additional data. In this research, a technique called unsupervised retrieval augmentation for cross-task learning is presented, where an initial model is expanded to include more accurate and relevant outputs derived from a knowledge repository. The knowledge repository is constructed through the analysis of input samples, and a strategy is developed to select high-quality derived outputs. As a result, the augmented model exhibits improved performance in a target task that differs from the original training tasks. Experiments with a large dataset demonstrate that this approach leads to notable improvements in various text-based tasks, including classification, sentiment analysis, and paragraph summarization. The developed method is efficient, scalable, and applicable to both large and small datasets. To facilitate further research, the code and knowledge repository for the experiments are made publicly available.

Optimizing hyperparameters in a differential privacy (DP) implementation for deep learning models through methods like grid search or random tuning can be computationally costly. Furthermore, the need to maintain private data usage increases the expense of this process exponentially. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach to hyperparameter optimization that combines the efficiency of gradient-free optimization with the privacy guarantees of DP. Leveraging the inherent properties of hyperparameters and learning rates, we develop a novel algorithm called Rate Gradient Descent (RGD) to enhance efficiency while maintaining privacy. Compared to alternative approaches, our method offers superior performance at a significantly lower cost. Experimental results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 demonstrate the effectiveness of RGD in multiple scenarios. Our findings provide a foundation for an efficient hyperparameter optimization framework that prioritizes privacy. To enhance the utility of our method, we outline potential avenues for future research aimed at further improving the performance of RGD. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-hu/RGD.

As a result, the effect of loss functions on performance is not well understood. This study investigates the impact of three commonly used loss functions - cross-entropy, hinge loss, and squared loss - on the performance of a neural network. It is observed that the behavior of these loss functions can be distinct, sometimes leading to unexpected outcomes. For instance, in some cases, cross-entropy loss does not necessarily result in a high accuracy, and hinge loss can yield better results even when the data is linearly separable. Additionally, this study delves into the theoretical aspects of loss functions and their relation to the optimization problem, and also explores the connection between loss functions and the activation functions used in neural networks. It is found that the choice of loss function can significantly affect the performance of a neural network, and that there is no single loss function that is universally superior. This study provides empirical and analytical insights into the effect of loss functions on neural network performance, and also offers a loss function analysis tool that can be used for further research into this topic. This study focuses on classification tasks, but the findings presented can be applied to other neural network applications as well. This research is an attempt to initiate further investigation into the complex behavior of loss functions in neural networks. This study is part of ongoing work aimed at developing a general framework for analyzing the effect of loss functions on neural network performance, and on exploring the connection between loss functions and deep learning architectures. This research focuses on modeling the mechanical effects of strain-induced crystallization in polyethylene through computational methods. Univariate strain-induced crystallization simulations have demonstrated significant increases in material stiffness and density, as well as formation of crystalline structures, in specific regions of polyethylene under mechanical stress. However, multivariate strain-induced crystallization simulations reveal a more complex picture, with multiple competing processes influencing the material's mechanical behavior and microstructure in different deformation scenarios. The model is validated through comparison with experimental data obtained from uniaxial and biaxial tension tests, and is subsequently employed to simulate the mechanical behavior and microstructure development of polyethylene under various loading conditions, including uniaxial tension, biaxial tension, and impact loading. The resulting simulations provide detailed insights into the spatial distribution of strain-induced crystallization, as well as the effects of stress, temperature, and chemical reaction rates on material microstructure and mechanical properties. The proposed model can be adapted for application to other semi-crystalline polymers subject to strain-induced crystallization. To advance the analysis of complex decision-making processes made by
artificial intelligence, we've assembled the Atlas of Machine Intelligence for
Complex Decision-making (ATOMIC). This atlas is a comprehensive, publicly
available database that structures diverse natural language descriptions of
causal relationships, incorporating multiple perspectives and levels of detail.
We introduce a novel framework for integrating and analyzing Causal Language
Graphs (CLGs), which are underlying structures representing the relationships

key elements from these descriptions, as well as a range of metrics to assess
the quality of generated text based on its embedded CLGs. To demonstrate the
utility of this framework, we developed a simple evaluation to gauge the
diversity of generated text through clg-based statistics. This evaluation can
be easily adapted for other text generation tasks. Our work on ATOMIC and its
associated evaluation tools is available at https://github.com/nyu-link/. Our

One of the most promising applications of quantum computing is the HHL linear algebra algorithm, which significantly outperforms its classical counterparts for certain large-scale linear algebra tasks. However, implementing HHL on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware is hindered by the need for universal amplitude amplification and re-preparation following the algorithm, which is challenging due to the lossy nature of quantum gates. In this study, we introduce NISQ-HHL, a modified HHL variant tailored for noisy quantum hardware, which replaces universal amplitude amplification with a targeted measurement strategy using a partial outcome specification. This version of the algorithm can successfully recover a linear operator for a given state, and we demonstrate its efficacy on a noisy quantum simulator by applying it to a simple linear algebra problem involving a small-scale state. Compared to the standard HHL algorithm, NISQ-HHL exhibits improved performance, with a 300-fold reduction in quantum gate executions required to recover the operator to a comparable level of accuracy. This modified HHL algorithm can be executed on a range of quantum devices, including the IBM Quantum Experience, and we provide a code implementation for this purpose. This variant of the HHL algorithm can be seen as an enhancement to the original HHL, and we propose a method for evaluating its performance based on a figure of merit known as the "effective precision" metric. This metric can be used to assess the performance of HHL on small-scale noisy quantum hardware, and we apply it to investigate the impact of different quantum hardware noise models on the efficacy of the HHL algorithm. This study highlights the importance of characterizing the noise inherent to the quantum hardware when evaluating the performance of HHL, and we provide a code implementation for calculating the effective precision of the HHL algorithm on a range of quantum hardware noise models. This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of a specific sequence related to parking functions, specifically those derived from the natural ordering of parking functions within the cube of side length $n$. We define $f_n$ as the smallest value $k$ such that the first $k$ positions of the lexicographic ordering of parking functions contain more than $n^n$ values. Our analysis examines the growth rate of $f_n$, demonstrating that $f_n$ is asymptotically equivalent to $2(\gamma+1)\cdot n \cdot \log n$ for an irrational, transcendental number $\gamma$ that arises as the asymptotic average of a particular random walk system and has a specific connection to the Euler-Mascheroni constant $\gamma_{\text{EM}}$. This asymptotic behavior can be reached through an iterative process that starts from a known baseline, specifically the asymptotic behavior of a related sequence known as the de Bruijn-Selberg statistic, which itself has a fascinating structure consisting of multiple nested layers of asymptotic behaviors. This discovery involves a novel application of a random walk asymptotic formula that has not been previously utilized in combinatorial contexts. Additionally, our findings provide a significant improvement over a prior bound established by the first author, with an order of magnitude difference. This research also introduces a new approach to analyzing the asymptotic behavior of parking function statistics, specifically an ergodic theory method that has not been previously applied in this field. This method will likely be applicable to the analysis of other parking function-related problems. This research was inspired by an earlier result established by Jukshith and the first author, which showed that the sum of the first $f_n$ positions of parking functions is asymptotically equivalent to $2(\gamma_{\text{EM}}+1)\cdot n^2 \cdot \log n$. This finding will likely be relevant to the study of certain random variables related to parking functions. This motivates an investigation of multilayer structures made from these materials. By combining first-principles calculations with a model of Heisenberg exchange, our study reveals that the magnetic properties at the interface between bismuth and cobalt can result in a unique Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, magnetoelastic effects, and spin-orbit coupling. By employing a modified Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative, we transform the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation into a solvable form, and then use the property of this derivative to convert the fractional potential into a non-fractional form, thereby obtaining an exact solution for the generalized Mie-type potential. This solution meets the boundary conditions of the $N$-dimensional harmonic oscillator, and includes the ground state and the first excited state solutions. This research extends previous works by Berruto et al. and Kajerling et al. by generalizing the potential from one-dimensional to $N$-dimensional space. Furthermore, we derive the fractional fractional Hamiltonian operator and the fractional fractional momentum operator, and show that the fractional momentum operator is Hermitian. Lastly, we discuss the relation between different fractional fractional derivative definitions, and the impact of these definitions on physical problems. This research demonstrates that the choice of fractional derivative definition significantly affects the Hamiltonian operator and the energy spectrum of the corresponding time-independent Schrödinger equation. This research also highlights the challenge of ensuring the Hermiticity of the momentum operator when using certain fractional derivative definitions, and the importance of carefully selecting these definitions to obtain physically meaningful energy spectra. This research provides a novel approach to solving the time-independent Schrödinger equation for a class of potentials that arise from the minimization of a functional, and demonstrates that the generalized Mie-type potential can be obtained through variational methods. We investigate how enforcing a network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In determining an upper bound for the network's Lipschitz constant, we analyze various common neural network architectures and identify that specific regularization techniques can provide such an upper bound. Subsequent experiments with training models using LipReg (a method for enforcing this constraint) show its effectiveness in preventing overfitting and improving performance when there is an insufficient amount of training data. However, as models become more complex and there is an abundance of training data, the performance with LipReg either declines or struggles to keep pace with traditional regularization methods. The potential issues with enforcing a global Lipschitz constant through optimization, along with various empirical evaluations, are also examined. We further explore local Lipschitz constants and find that optimizing the average of these values over the training set yields performance comparable to, if not better than, traditional regularized models. This improvement is particularly evident when models are complex and there is an abundance of training data. We also examine the relationship between these constants and the quality of the solutions obtained. Lastly, we discuss the connection between these constants and the recently introduced robust accuracy measure, showing that the latter can be seen as the minimum local Lipschitz constant over the training set. We further explore local Lipschitz constants in the context of adversarial training and find that the distribution of these constants provides a more nuanced view of the robustness of the models than the corresponding robust accuracy values. We demonstrate this in figures illustrating the distribution of these constants for models trained with different adversarial attack methods. We also examine the efficacy of our approach in reducing the Lipschitz constant for models trained with adversarial training. We conclude by discussing the implications of our results and potential future directions of research. We have made our code publicly available at https://github.com/strivers96/LipReg. To address the mystery of the Lepton Flavor, we propose a new, non-decoupled, third-generation gauge vector leptoquark, denoted as $T_3$, which transforms under the $SU(3)_c \otimes SU(2)_L \otimes U(1)_Y$ symmetry according to $q_{L,3}T_3$, $l_{L,3}T_3$, and $T_3^{\dagger}T_3$. We examine $T_3$ in various mass regimes and gauge boson, fermion, and leptoquark interactions, identifying relevant production and decay processes. For the case where $T_3$ is heavy, pair production via slepton or quark fusion is the dominant process. For lighter $T_3$, single production via $W$ or $Z$ boson fusion becomes significant. We calculate the cross-sections for these processes at next-to-leading order in QCD, incorporating higher-order logarithmic corrections and parton shower effects. We also establish upper bounds on $T_3$ mass based on its decay into $W$, $Z$, top quark, bottom quark, tau lepton, or neutrinos. For instance, for a lifetime of $10^{-13}$ s, these limits are 1.4 TeV, 1.3 TeV, 1.1 TeV, 0.8 TeV, 0.7 TeV, and 400 GeV for $T_3$ with the same charge as the top quark, and 1.5 TeV, 1.4 TeV, 1.2 TeV, 0.8 TeV, 0.7 TeV, and 450 GeV for $T_3$ with the same charge as the tau lepton. Quantifying radiation exposure in low-dose PET imaging poses a significant challenge due to the large variability in image quality resulting from different scan protocols. To address this challenge, a new uncertainty-aware neural network has been developed to reduce radiation exposure during PET imaging. This new method, known as PET-ScoreNet, utilizes a hybrid network that integrates a contrast-enhanced image and an uncertainty map to accurately assess image quality. This assessment enables optimized scan protocols that minimize radiation exposure while maintaining acceptable diagnostic standards. Experimental results using a real-world dataset demonstrated that the PET-ScoreNet model effectively prioritized image quality and reduced radiation exposure by 25% relative to conventional protocols. Furthermore, the model proved robust in evaluating images acquired at doses outside its training range, indicating its clinical utility in guiding optimized protocols across various imaging scenarios. The code for PET-ScoreNet is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ahmedhammami/PET-ScoreNet. A key concept in coreference resolution involves identifying when two mentions refer to the same entity, often relying on the structural relationship between mentions in a sentence. The centering theory proposes a framework for predicting these relationships based on pragmatic principles, suggesting that speakers prefer certain entities as a "center" of attention. This study investigates whether incorporating features from the centering theory into neural coreference models can improve their performance. Experiments using the BART model on three datasets show that incorporating these features generally enhances performance, with a 0.38 F-score improvement on the easiest dataset but no significant gain on the more challenging ones. A related analysis of the model's representations reveals that it inherently captures similar information to the centering features, which may limit the benefits of explicit feature incorporation. Despite this, the study highlights the value of the centering theory in guiding the development of better coreference models.

The beam breakup instability poses a significant threat to the performance of Energy Recovery Linacs, particularly those employing long magnetic lattices. Studies have shown that beam-loaded microwave radiation in a filling design can either exacerbate or counteract BBU, yet the underlying causes of this variability are not yet fully understood. This investigation delves into the causes of this behavior by examining the impact of filling designs on the beam-loaded microwave radiation within a model ERL lattice. It is demonstrated that the beam-loaded microwave radiation can be either amplified or diminished by designing the filling pattern to either align with or counteract the natural oscillations of the lattice, thus providing a fundamental approach to mitigating the beam breakup instability issue. Building upon the underlying structure of the color algebra within $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory, we derive a key component of scattering amplitudes known as the one-loop central-emission vertex for two gluons. This vertex serves as a fundamental object in the "amplitude on shell" formulation, where it represents the sum of two gluon scattering amplitudes added to the counterterm, divided by the overall factor of the squared gluon mass. By examining the symmetries of the scattering amplitude and utilizing the properties of BPS invariants, we derive an explicit expression for the two-gluon central-emission vertex and verify its accuracy through comparison with existing literature. Furthermore, we outline a straightforward path to deriving the scattering amplitude from the central-emission vertex, achieving this result through a previously unknown route. Additionally, we explore the implications of our findings for the three-gluon case. Or rather, we initially aim to do so, however, encounter an obstacle in deriving the three-gluon vertex due to an unanticipated complexity in the resulting expression for the scattering amplitude, which in turn appears more difficult to interpret than expected. Nonetheless, we do offer an alternate, simpler approach to understanding the three-gluon scattering amplitude through a related object known as the tricolor number, which in turn is linked to the BPS invariants and possesses a specific symmetry under the CPT transformation. This tricolor number can be obtained through a direct calculation of the scattering amplitude, and in the case of the one-loop four-gluon scattering amplitude, it takes on a particular form that consists of multiple components, each associated with distinct helicity configurations of the scattered gluons. Theories about highly stretched polymer brushes have been extensively studied and can now be applied to complex, irregular surfaces. However, there's still a lack of understanding regarding the localized regions within these surfaces that are excluded to polymer chains. Recent simulations suggest that in highly stretched brushes, even complex surfaces have generally uniform excluded volume regions when normalized by their curvature. Based on these findings, we've developed a general framework for analyzing the excluded volume regions in molten polymer brushes of any shape, using a curved surface version of the Gaussian approximation. By integrating this approximation, we can determine the probability distribution of polymer chains within these surfaces. Notably, our approach indicates that in the limit of strongly stretched brushes, there are no areas completely excluded to polymer chains, instead, the probability of chain localization in these areas decreases exponentially with the brush's thickness-to-chain length ratio. Our results provide a comprehensive, analytically tractable model of strongly stretched polymer brushes of any shape, offering insights into the behavior of polymer chains within them.

A positive integer vector's representation of a point in n-dimensional space consists of the distances from that point to n fixed points, known as landmarks. A set of vectors is considered fully detecting for a set of points if every point in the set maps to a unique vector. The minimum number of vectors required for this condition to be met is known as the metric dimension of the set of points. We analyze the trimmed metric dimension, a new parameter that counts the number of vectors in a fully detecting set, minus the number of points that map to the same vector as another point in the set. We explore the relationship between the trimmed metric dimension and the metric dimension of a graph's vertex set, examining how it changes in response to the addition of new vertices or edges to an existing graph. We also establish lower and upper bounds for the trimmed metric dimension of a graph with a given number of vertices, as well as landmarks. Furthermore, we investigate the trimming of a graph's metric dimension when the set of landmarks changes. Additionally, we look at the added value of new vertices or edges in this context. Lastly, we provide an illustrative example of an infinite family of graphs with an exponential gap between their metric and trimmed dimensions. This is in contrast to previous research, where an infinite family of graphs with a polynomial gap between their metric and trimmed dimensions cannot exist. We conclude by suggesting a more general approach to the trimmed metric dimension parameter, proposing the use of a function to capture its behavior rather than a single value. This is particularly relevant for infinite graphs where the trimmed metric dimension may vary and cannot be simplified to a single value. We term this new parameter the trimmed dimension of a set of points or a graph, and explore its properties including its response to changes in the set of points or the added vertices and edges in a graph. We also examine the relationship between the trimmed dimension of a graph and the number of its vertices. We note that the trimmed dimension of an infinite graph may be more complex and cannot be captured by a single value, requiring further exploration. We provide an initial approach to the study of the trimmed dimension of infinite graphs by constructing a compact representation of the vector space of an infinite graph. We achieve this by using a set of landmark vertices that map to unique vectors for all points in the graph, and we term these landmark vertices the generating set of the graph. Using a neural network, we've created a highly detailed map of gamma-ray emissions from the sky. Based on 8 years of data from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, this new map has a 10 times higher resolution than previous versions. We've also developed an algorithm to identify variable sources more effectively, which has been applied to the same data set. This has led to the discovery of over 160 new candidate sources exhibiting variability. Together with existing lists of sources, this has expanded the catalog to over 2500 variable sources, with over 1000 showing-day scale variability for the first time. This enhanced map and variable source catalog are valuable tools for future missions and multi-wavelength studies. Additionally, the developed neural network provides a more efficient method for removing non-variable sources from large data sets. We've made the map, variable source catalog, and associated data sets available for public use. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of neural networks in analyzing large data sets and highlights areas for further research, such as determining the causes of variability in some sources. We searched archival images from the Pan-STARRS1 survey for binary asteroid candidates by analyzing the light curves of over 1.5 million asteroids with well-defined orbits. We identified 57 potential binary asteroid candidates with orbital periods ranging from 0.006 to 5.6 days in light curves that showed a significant periodic variation. Notably, only one candidate exhibited a double-peaked light curve, which is a hallmark of a tidally locked binary asteroid with a synchronized rotation period. We propose that the majority of our detected periodic variables are likely to be single asteroids with non-synchronous rotation periods, which could be a common phenomenon in the asteroid belt. We also suggest that future observations with higher sensitivity and resolution, such as with the Large Synthesis Telescope, may be able to confirm the rotation periods and phase curves of these asteroids in a single observation. Our findings imply that many main belt asteroids may have large amplitude non-synchronous rotation, which could be a precursor to binary formation through rotational breakup. Our search yielded 11 previously known binary asteroids with long-sided orbital periods, which we verified by analyzing their light curves and orbital parameters. Our data set has been made publicly available on the APOD4CASSI website. Our study highlights the potential of searching light curves for clues about an asteroid's physical properties and rotation history, and the need for a more comprehensive survey of the asteroid population using a telescope with a larger field of view. Our results also raise questions about the binary formation mechanisms in the asteroid belt and the stability of non-synchronous rotation in large asteroids. Our study has implications for future missions such as the Lucy and Europa Clipper missions, which will study binary asteroids and non-synchronous rotation in the Trojan and Hildas asteroids. This research supplements the paper titled "Identification and Estimation of a Partially Linear Regression Model using Network Data: Inference and an Application to Network Peer Influences." It explores a partially linear regression model within the context of social network data. Such models incorporate both linear and nonlinear components in the regression equation. The nonlinear component represents complex interactions, whereas the linear part enables the estimation of average effects. We establish that under certain conditions, the partial linear model can be identified using network data. Furthermore, we develop an estimation approach based on the local quadratic method and the network's characteristics. The results of a Monte Carlo simulation are presented, and an empirical analysis of peer influences within a high school social network is conducted. The latter reveals both positive and negative peer effects existing among students. The study highlights the importance of considering both linear and nonlinear components when modeling peer effects. The empirical findings also demonstrate that the model's ability to capture both positive and negative influences is crucial. The research presented can be expanded to other contexts involving network data and multiple regression. The paper concludes by outlining potential avenues for such an expansion. The supplementary material includes additional information regarding model identification, estimation, inference, and Monte Carlo simulation design. The empirical analysis and data used in the study are also detailed. The R code for the Monte Carlo simulation and empirical analysis is provided in the appendix. The data and code for the study are available at https://www.dropbox.com/s/6m6m6m6m6m6m6m6m6m/PLMRN.RData?dl=0. The R code for the study is also available at https://github.com/username/PLMRN. Building on the success of a previous study that extended the Leibniz rule to a fractional integral and derivative for fractions of order alpha, we generalize this rule to the variable-order Riemann-Liouville fractional integral and derivative. By defining new operators, we establish two versions of the Leibniz rule: one for the variable-order fractional integral and derivative, and a modified version for the variable-order fractional derivative alone. These rules take all possible fraction orders into account, providing a more flexible tool for problem-solving. A key discovery is that we can alternate between different fraction orders by switching the order of integration and differentiation. A specific example involving a variable-order fractional derivative of an exponential function is also included. This generalization is expected to expand the scope of problems that can be tackled using the variable-order fractional approach. A previous study on the type of the Bernoulli polynomial under the fractional integral operator is also extended to the variable-order setting, revealing that the variable-order fractional integral operator preserves the type of an analytic function. This finding is further demonstrated with examples of variable-order Apolliez, Strohni, and Louiville types of functions. This research is an ongoing effort to explore the variable-order fractional setting for a wide range of applications, including nonlinear problems and differential equations. We present a novel approach to guiding players through an open-world text adventure game using a simplified Dungeons and Dragons framework. Our method employs a theory-of-mind inspired strategy to assign player characters to different roles, which we believe is a first for artificial intelligence in this domain. To achieve this, we developed a multi-task learning model that combines text classification and conversational dialogue tasks. Specifically, we trained a model to predict player intentions and assign roles to them, as well as a separate conversation model using a mixture of actor-observer theory-of-mind. By integrating these models using a weighted average, we created a unified model capable of guiding multiple players with diverse intentions in a coherent and engaging narrative. Our approach is supported by an extensive dataset of D&D conversations, comprising over 35,000 turns of text. We demonstrated our approach's effectiveness by guiding multiple players through a procedurally generated city, each with their own unique goal, using a lightweight Dungeons and Dragons ruleset. Our results show that our method can successfully balance the interests of multiple players, each with their own unique agenda, in a text-based adventure game. Our code and dataset are available online at https://github.com/nyu DAL. Systems. Learn. Challenge. Website. at. https://sites.google.com/view/dal-systems-learning-challenge-2023.

The presence of topological knots in biological molecules like proteins has sparked both scientific interest and debate. Although methods to detect knots are not universally agreed upon, indications of knots have been linked to various biological implications, including protein stability and interactions. Using a knot-detection approach based on polymer models, we examined the possible twisted structures of 160 indicator proteins and found that in many cases, multiple cross-over trajectories could be selected as the most plausible from their native states. By analyzing these results with topological invariants, we found that the chosen trajectories often reflected complex, intertwined knots, and that the most frequent knots were associated with specific protein classes, such as G-proteins. Our findings suggest that the twisted structures of proteins may be more complex than previously thought and that the diversity of knots could be linked to specific biological functions. Our research also highlights the utility of using cross-over trajectories in polymer models to investigate the knotted states of biological molecules. Our findings are supported by recent studies suggesting that the detection methods used here may overestimate the prevalence of knots, but not their complexity. Our approach to analyzing the twisted structures of proteins may be applicable to other biological molecules with recurring closed loops. Our code for detecting knots is available online. Recent advancements in large language models have led to increased performance in various supervised tasks, yet the potential benefits of unsupervised learning from hypothetical scenarios, particularly phrasal conditional instances, have not been fully explored. Our proposed approach, DISCO, leverages a large language model through a distillation process, specifically targeting these conditional phrases. We gather a large dataset of 39,000 phrasal conditional instances across diverse topics and present a method to distill this knowledge into a 512-dimensional vector. By utilizing this vector in a classifier, we achieve a 12% improvement in the F1 score compared to a baseline using a mean pooling strategy. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates increased robustness against adversarial attacks and an 8% increase in the Celebes Human Edited Adversarial dataset's F1 score. System-level modifications using our distilled vector also yield a 5% improvement in the F1 score on the SARDI dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/nyk157/disco.

A striking phenomenon in epitaxy is its capacity to transform a non-reactive substrate into an ideal match for film growth through the formation of a reactive interface with the air gap between layers. This complex behavior can manifest in remote epitaxy, pinhole epitaxy, or van der Waals epitaxy. Our research used ab initio calculations in conjunction with scanning tunneling microscopy and Raman spectroscopy to explore the epitaxial relationships between Heusler films grown on a graphene/sapphire substrate. By examining three different Heusler compounds, we found that their epitaxial relationships can be either remote, or can be controlled through chemical modifications of the graphene layer above, thereby shifting between remote and van der Waals epitaxy. This shift from a 2D to a 3D interface can be precisely controlled to achieve either a clean air interface essential for van der Waals epitaxy, or a reactive interface necessary for remote epitaxy. This level of control over the epitaxial relationship through chemical modification of the graphene layer above, combined with the minimal lattice mismatch between Heusler compounds and graphene, makes it possible to design a wide range of Heusler compounds that can exhibit both remote and van der Waals epitaxy on sapphire substrates. This breakthrough paves the way for precise control over the growth of Heusler compounds on sapphire substrates, and highlights the potential for growing a wide range of films that exhibit both remote and van der Waals epitaxy on graphene-covered substrates. This discovery also underscores the significance of considering multiple interfaces in complex epitaxial systems, and the potential for chemical modification of the air gap between layers to influence the growth of films. The growing popularity of wearable devices for health monitoring necessitates the integration of machine learning models into mobile devices, while maintaining user privacy. However, constraints on local storage, memory, and computation pose significant challenges for training and deploying effective machine learning models. To address these limitations, we propose FedHealth, a federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare that enables the efficient training of models without compromising data privacy. This approach allows models to be rapidly adapted to new environments through knowledge transferred from other locations without the need for retraining. We evaluate FedHealth using real-world data from wearable devices and find that it outperforms the local training method, reducing computation costs by 7.4 times while maintaining a classification accuracy of 80% within 5 iterations. This improvement is attributed to the slow decline in learning rates during federated learning, which can be accelerated by increasing the client batch size. This approach has broader applications in various fields such as healthcare, finance, and finance-technology industries. From the introduction of the first SEIR model by Kermack and McKendrick in 1927 to more advanced models incorporating factors such as asymptomatic cases, demographics, and temporal changes, we review notable models and their applications. Although the pandemic has presented numerous challenges, including determining the exact transmission rate and estimating the proportion of asymptomatic cases, researchers have employed a range of data sources, including contact tracing, hospitalization records, and serological surveys, to inform their models. By examining both past and present research, this report aims to offer insights for future epidemic control strategies. As the pandemic continues to evolve, with new variants emerging and changing behavior among the population, there is a growing need for models that can adapt quickly to these changes. In response, we outline a range of models that can be easily updated, including models that utilize data from the early stages of the pandemic, as well as suggestions for future research, including the integration of psychological factors into models and the development of machine learning models that can provide real-time predictions. With the pandemic now entering its third year, there is a pressing need for models that can provide accurate forecasts of future cases, hospitalizations, and deaths. In this report, we review the sources of uncertainty in pandemic forecasting, including the variability of transmission rates, the effectiveness of vaccines, and the impact of government interventions. We also discuss the role of big data in forecasting, as well as the potential for machine learning models to provide real-time predictions. In the final section, we outline a range of future research directions, including the development of models that can account for the effects of long-term immunity, the integration of psychological factors into models, and the use of machine learning models to provide real-time predictions. We conclude by emphasizing the importance of continued collaboration between mathematicians, epidemiologists, and policymakers in the fight against the pandemic. A major advantage of this approach is the ability to generate high-resolution data from lower-resolution datasets across a wide range of Re values, even for complex, three-dimensional turbulent flows. A key finding also emerged from the analysis of turbulent flow at a Re value of 10^6, where it was discovered that the distribution of the smallest eddies approaches a critical value of around 60% of the characteristic length of the flow, regardless of the actual Re value. The field of reinforcement learning has seen significant advancements in recent years, particularly in the realm of highly complex and ever-changing tasks. To further improve reinforcement learning strategies, particularly those for continuous learning, a controlled and comprehensive evaluation framework is essential. To address this need, we present L2Explorer, a cutting-edge evaluation platform that enables the assessment of multiple lifelong reinforcement learning approaches across diverse, dynamically generated scenarios. This environment, characterized by multiple, sequentially encountered exploration tasks with varying structures, allows for rigorous evaluation of reinforcement learning agents under conditions of uncertainty, including changes in task layout, obstacles, and reward prioritization. To facilitate meaningful comparisons, we provide pre-trained agents for each of the 18 unique exploration tasks in L2Explorer, as well as tools for automating the creation of new tasks and evaluating reinforcement learning agents against established benchmarks. L2Explorer is an open-source platform available on GitHub, offering users a flexible platform for designing custom evaluation protocols and evaluating new reinforcement learning approaches. The positive correlation between galaxy stellar mass and star formation rate (SFR) breaks down for the most massive galaxies, and our understanding of this phenomenon is limited. Using a sample of 1766 galaxies with a wide range of masses, from $10^{7.5}$ to $10^{11.5}$ M$_\odot$, we investigate the SFR-mass relation in local galaxies. For a subset of 1436 star-forming galaxies without an active galactic nucleus (AGN), we find that the slope of the SFR-mass relation becomes less positive at high masses, with a mass range that depends on the specific SFR (sSFR). For example, this transition occurs at $\sim 10^{10.5}$ M$_\odot$ for galaxies with a sSFR of $10^{-10.5}$ yr$^{-1}$. We also examine the relation in 330 galaxies with an AGN, and find that the presence of an AGN can influence the shape of the SFR-mass relation, with a more gradual decline in slope for these galaxies. We propose that a combination of factors, including the role of AGN, gas supply, and the efficiency of galaxy bulges, contribute to the turnover in the SFR-mass relation at high masses. We suggest that the relationship between specific SFR and mass provides a framework for understanding these processes, and that it may be influenced by a mass range over which bulge growth is most significant, with a lower edge that depends on the sSFR of the galaxy. We also explore the implications of our findings for the growth of galaxy bulges, and the role of major mergers in driving bulge growth. We note that the mass range over which the SFR-mass relation turns over may be influenced by selection effects, and that further study of this phenomenon will require a more comprehensive understanding of the selection effects that govern the availability of local galaxy populations. We also provide a simple analytical model of the SFR-mass relation, and discuss the limitations of this model. We conclude by noting that the study of the SFR-mass relation in local galaxies is a rich area of investigation, and that further study of this phenomenon will require a combination of observational and theoretical approaches. We also provide a list of suggested targets for future galaxy populations that we can study with upcoming surveys, and that will provide a deeper understanding of the processes that govern the growth of galaxy bulges. A pervasive challenge in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) is addressing the numerous incorrect relationships present in training data. Since VRD involves modeling both objects and their relationships, it is essential to tackle this issue effectively. We propose a new approach, Relationship Re-scoring with Group Attention (RRGA), that addresses this problem by utilizing a dual attention mechanism to differentiate between instances of the same relationship type. This leads to a significant improvement in accuracy, with a 3.5% absolute gain over the current state-of-the-art on the VOC2012 dataset. RRGA also exhibits robust performance under limited training data, achieving a 5.6% absolute gain in the setting with 10% reduced data. To further enhance model performance, we introduce a simple yet effective way to augment training data by introducing a random relationship type swap, known as Relation Type Swap (RTS). This technique is universally applicable to VRD tasks. With RRGA, RTS, and an additional 10% reduced data, we attain a 7.5% absolute gain over the current top-performing method. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangyin/RRGA.

The observation of a rapidly rotating young star, likely born with a disk, presents a puzzle given the expected slowdown from conservation of angular momentum during disk dissipation. To understand this rotation enhancement, we investigated the $K_2$-episodic photometry and spectroscopic data of HN Tauri, revealing a rotation period of under 7.5 days and varying brightness over 11.5 days. This period system includes an unusually short orbital period of 8.5 days, suggesting a companion with a mass similar to that of Jupiter, as well as an equatorial rotation velocity of 12 km/s. By analyzing the star's properties and comparing it to theoretical models, we found that its current rotation rate is significantly higher than predicted based on conservation of angular momentum. This discrepancy could be explained by an internal differential rotation, or alternatively, might result from the dissipation of angular momentum in a disk that has been depleted, potentially leading to the consumption of a massive Jupiter-mass planet. This possible planetary consumption could have implications for theories of planetary migration and the ultimate fate of massive exoplanets. Alternatively, an internal rotation gradient could be indicative of a complex internal dynamics within the star. This scenario may also be representative of a broader population of rapidly rotating young stars with rapidly spinning surfaces. This study highlights the value of photometric variability in the study of young rotating stars and their surrounding environments. Quantum mechanics governs the behavior of matter at its most fundamental level, yet the intricate interplay of multiple degrees of freedom often leads to complex phenomena that defy straightforward interpretation. In silicon, the coexistence of electron spin and orbital (valley) degrees of freedom presents both opportunities and challenges for device functionality. To gain a deeper understanding of this interplay, researchers used scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy to directly observe the interference patterns resulting from electron scattering off impurities in silicon surfaces. By analyzing these interference patterns in individual atoms, the team was able to observe the swapping of spin and orbital degrees of freedom at the atomic scale, a phenomenon known as "valley-spin mixing." This discovery provides a new perspective on silicon's inherent properties and highlights the potential for highly versatile silicon devices that can take advantage of this interplay of degrees of freedom. This finding also highlights the capabilities of low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy in directly observing the intricate behavior of electrons in materials. Complex systems, characterized by intricate relationships and dynamic interactions across multiple components, pose significant challenges in modeling their behavior using traditional methods. Working with categorical data for model selection and variable reduction is a common challenge in various high-dimensional applications. Despite the Group Lasso's effectiveness for this purpose, its limitations become apparent when dealing with polyedral-based regression models and multi-category data. Specifically, the L1-penalty's failure to adapt to differing variable importance weights can result in the simultaneous elimination of multiple relevant categories. This paper addresses this issue by presenting a data-driven approach to modify the Group Lasso, referred to as the Adaptive Group Lasso via Iterative Thresholding (AGIT), which employs iterative re-weighting and thresholding of local L1 penalties to adapt to the scale of individual groups. This adaptation enables the efficient selection and reduction of multi-category data within the framework of the Elastic Net. Experimental results based on real and simulated datasets demonstrate AGIT's efficacy and the benefits of its adaptive nature. This approach is particularly relevant for addressing challenges in the analysis of multi-category data, network inference, and collaborative filtering. The code for AGIT is publicly available on GitHub. The Adaptive Group Lasso via Iterative Thresholding (AGIT) can be used with the R package elastnet. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on various tasks, yet their reliance on vast amounts of general-purpose data makes it challenging to tailor them for specific domains. To address this limitation, we propose a method to inject structured knowledge into pre-trained language models using type of constraints, including rules, graphs, and tables. By applying this method to multiple domains, we demonstrate a significant improvement in task accuracy, with an average increase of 12% across five different domains. Furthermore, our approach shows that it is possible to transfer knowledge to a single shot from just one example, with performance surpassing the state-of-the-art in few-shot learning. Our code and models are publicly available at github.com/google/structured-knowledge-injection.

This paper addresses this challenge by introducing an efficient AA rendering method for line joins. This method employs a lookup table to rapidly determine the AA pattern based on the join type and map scale. As a result, this approach enables the use of AA rendering on line joins for large-scale vector maps without sacrificing performance. The growing interest in 360-degree virtual tourism videos necessitates the development of effective methods to predict viewers' perspectives. This research explores a novel approach to predicting perspective by utilizing video subtitles. Initially, a subtitle extraction module is employed to obtain the current subtitle, which is then matched with previously encountered subtitles to determine similar scenes. The strategy is particularly beneficial for reducing perspective change prediction during video segments without significant updates. The proposed approach focuses on predicting perspective changes during subtitle-based modification periods. Experimental evaluations using a custom-built dataset reveal that subtitle-based prediction outperforms state-of-the-art methods in certain scenarios, achieving a 10.6% improvement in the CIE2002 metric. As another assessment, the method is applied to regular 2D videos, achieving a 6.8% increase in the CIE2002 metric. We find that even without taking into account non-perturbative effects, the estimated uncertainty from the leading infrared renormalon already reaches a few percent by $x \sim 10^{-3}$. Furthermore, we determine the non-perturbative coefficient for the TMD PDF at small $x$ and identify a suitable non-perturbative parameterization to describe the dipole TMD PDF, especially in regions where $x$ is small. Our findings are particularly relevant for the small-$x$ TMD PDF in proton-proton collisions, especially in forward rapidity regions, and may be particularly useful for predicting final states involving small-$x$ gluons, such as in forward neutron production off proton-proton scattering. Using a pre-existing, generic model can significantly expedite and reduce costs of developing a bespoke model for new tasks by simply reusing existing ones with little to no additional training. However, relying on such a model for guidance often requires access to labeled data, which contradicts the purpose of leveraging existing knowledge efficiently. This paper presents a novel approach to circumvent this issue by utilizing an untrained model to rank previously considered options among a set, without needing to know the correct target. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on multiple datasets by successfully employing a generic model in a manner that is effectively a "black-box," thereby achieving comparable performance to models trained on smaller subsets of the available data. Furthermore, our method exhibits flexibility in being able to handle both classification and ranking tasks, and we show that it can be applied to multiple domains with minimal modifications. The code for our approach has been made publicly available on GitHub.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module can be a computationally challenging task, especially for modules related to algebraic structures like group algebras and quiver representations. However, when a module has a simple composition series, its lattice structure can be determined via Krull-Schmidt invariants. For modules that are multiplicity-free, their lattice of submodules can be more easily determined, as any submodule automatically has a multiplicity-free composition series. As a result, research focuses on efficiently calculating the lattice of submodules for multiplicity-free modules using various approaches, such as analyzing the module's underlying algebraic structure or employing combinatorial methods to construct the lattice from partial module or submodule data. This talk will cover the concepts and techniques for constructing the lattice of submodules for multiplicity-free modules, including examples and the use of the software NMBD. Additionally, we will discuss the differences between using quiver representations and group algebras in module lattices. This approach can also be applied to related structures like poset algebras and cluster-tilting modules. Finally, we will outline some open problems and potential research directions. This talk aims to appeal to a broad audience by minimizing prerequisites, as it assumes only a basic understanding of lattice theory and algebra. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly in many scenarios. In this research, we introduce a novel framework called Co-Imitation Training (CoIT) that leverages multiple agents learning together in a reinforcement learning setting. Each agent's learning is motivated by a desire to excel at a different task, yet they share the same environment and credit assignment system. As a result, their individual learning processes are influenced by the others' performance, leading to a balance of their relative performances. We demonstrate through experiments that this mutual influence accelerates learning, enhances robustness, and leads to better performance compared to traditional reinforcement learning alone. Moreover, we show that this framework can be applied to a range of scenarios beyond our core study. Systematic evaluations reveal that CoIT's effectiveness stems from an equilibrium state where the performance differences between the agents are minimized, and this state is reached more efficiently than alone. This is further supported by an analysis of the policy space. We also explore an extension to a multi-task setting, and discuss several potential future directions for this research. All code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyang-wang/CoIT.

This issue becomes particularly pronounced when the action space is extensively large, as seen in translation tasks. To address this limitation, we propose a novel efficient reinforcement learning framework, known as batch policy optimization, that significantly minimizes the needed decoy instances while maintaining the learning rate of traditional methods. This approach takes advantage of the latent representation of the encoder to train a single set of policy parameters across multiple translations from the same input. Our experiments on two large translation datasets demonstrate a substantial decrease in the computational expense and a boost in the translation quality. This approach also shows the potential to be applicable to other large action space reinforcement learning tasks beyond neural machine translation. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, NoSQL database that employs a transactional protocol known as multi-document atomic transactions. In order to analyze the coherence of a system's transactional protocol, it is essential to examine the relationships between version vectors used for conflict detection and the protocol's specification of read and write effects. In the case of MongoDB, the documentation of its transactional protocol is relatively limited, and determining its coherence requires an in-depth examination of the version vector algebra and protocol specification. 

In our research, we delved into the internals of MongoDB's transactional protocol and verified its coherence using a formal approach. Specifically, we extracted a mathematical representation of the protocol's version vector algebra and validated that it conforms to a specific, well-established property known as "serializability" or "atomicity". In addition, we examined the transactional protocols supported by MongoDB, including the latest version of MongoDB 5.0, and demonstrated that they maintain coherence. 

Our research provides a clear and step-by-step analysis of MongoDB's transactional protocol, starting from an introduction to version vector algebra, through an examination of MongoDB's protocol, to an assessment of its coherence. This approach can be applied to the analysis of other databases employing similar transactional protocols. Our findings have been made publicly available through a formal verification framework known as "Moon". In our paper, we also discuss the challenges we encountered in examining MongoDB's documentation and provide suggestions for improving the documentation of transactional protocols used in databases.

Unlike previous approaches that focus on making models invariant to certain transformations, TPC guarantees that the impact of unwanted variations is minimized. This guarantee is ensured by introducing a unique performance metric for each model, which accounts for the effects of desired and undesired transformations. We utilize this metric to develop an optimization problem that smooths the model to maximize performance differences in desired versus undesired transformation scenarios. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as biology, electricity networks, and finance, is a critical task that can be accomplished using dynamic clustering methods. These clusters represent groups of systems that behave in the same way under similar conditions and can indicate a system's stability or provide targets for control. However, most existing clustering techniques require the specification of important parameters by experts, which can lead to suboptimal results. This paper proposes a novel, data-driven approach called IICDC for expert-independent clustering in complex dynamic systems. IICDC utilizes impact and connection graphs, which can be readily obtained from time-series data, to create a robust and efficient method for clustering. This approach minimizes the impact of parameter sensitivity and provides a more accurate representation of the system's dynamics. We validate IICDC through synthetic and real-world data, including a famous biological model and two financial networks. Compared to existing methods, IICDC demonstrates superior performance and more accurate results. This approach offers a flexible tool for researchers and practitioners to explore complex dynamic systems with little prior knowledge. This approach is available as an open-source tool on GitHub. This work is an extension of our previous conference paper presented at IJCAI 2020. This paper includes additional results, new financial data, and a detailed example of the algorithm's implementation. This paper is also accompanied by supplementary materials including raw data, impact estimation codes, and additional figures and tables. To improve the security of language models in sensitive applications like natural language processing, a new framework called SparseGAN has been developed to counter model-based adversarial attacks by minimizing both the norm and the difference between the generated samples and genuine data. This results in a two-class game where the generator produces samples in one class and the attacker aims to shift them to the other. Evaluating this framework on text generation using a new metric shows that SparseGAN significantly enhances robustness without compromising performance, and outperforms standard training on several datasets including a newly introduced robust dataset.
